title: Indian Markets Face Volatile Week as Q1 Earnings Collide With Oil Surge and Global Tech Selloff
excerpt: HSBC upgrades Sensex target to 84,000 as foreign investors return, but rising crude prices and Iran war cloud the outlook for the week ahead.
body:
• Indian markets face a volatile week with Q1 earnings from heavyweights like Reliance and ICICI Bank, rising oil prices above $86 a barrel, and a global tech selloff all competing for investor attention.
  • HSBC upgraded Indian equities to "neutral" from "underweight," raising its Sensex year-end target to 84,000, citing easing crude prices and returning foreign flows.
  • India's June CPI hit 4.38% — the highest since December 2024 — as the US-Iran war pushes transport and energy costs higher, narrowing the RBI's room to cut rates at its August meeting.
  • Foreign investors turned net buyers in July with $1.6 billion in purchases after four months of selling totaling $27.7 billion, but analysts warn sustainability depends on how the Middle East conflict evolves.

Six Forces Shaping the Week

Indian stocks enter the week of July 21 caught between competing currents. The Nifty 50 closed last week at 24,072.75 and the Sensex at 77,186.87, both effectively flat on Thursday as IT gains offset a post-results drop in financials. Traders are waiting for a decisive trigger, and this week offers several.

The immediate catalyst is Q1 earnings. Results from HDFC Bank, which reported a 5% rise in quarterly profit to ₹19,060 crore, and Tech Mahindra, which posted a 28% profit surge, set the tone last week. This week brings Reliance Industries, ICICI Bank, and a wave of mid-cap reporters. How management teams characterize demand — particularly any commentary on the Iran war's impact on margins — will shape positioning.

"HSBC upgraded Indian equities to "neutral" from "underweight" last week, raising its 2026 Sensex year-end target to 84,000 — suggesting an 8.6% upside from current levels."

Oil and the Iran Overhang

Brent crude climbed above $86 a barrel on Friday, up over 10% for the week, after the US-Iran ceasefire collapsed on July 7 and both sides escalated to infrastructure targeting. Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint for one-fifth of global oil, has fallen to two-month lows.

For India, the world's third-largest crude importer, a sustained oil spike directly pressures the import bill, the rupee, and corporate margins across energy-dependent sectors. India's June CPI surged to 4.38%, the highest since December 2024, with transport inflation rebounding to 4.31% — a sign the Middle East energy shock is now feeding through into consumer prices.

At the wholesale level, the WPI hit a fresh all-time high of 9.87% in June, driven by mineral oils and basic metals. Together, these readings materially narrow the Reserve Bank of India's room to ease rates at its August Monetary Policy Committee meeting.

"Indian markets are delicately poised, with a host of moving parts set to influence the next leg of the trend. A decisive breakout is likely only if the monsoon deficit narrows and tensions around the Iran conflict ease."

— Amnish Aggarwal, Co-Head of Institutional Equities, PL Capital

Global Tech Selloff Casts a Shadow

The Nasdaq 100 took a hit last week as profit-taking followed inflated expectations for a stellar earnings season. IBM's below-estimate second-quarter revenue guidance dragged India's IT index down 0.7% mid-week. With Alphabet, Tesla, and other US tech giants reporting this week, any further disappointment could ripple through Indian IT stocks, which make up a significant Nifty weight.

The rotation matters for India. HSBC noted that the foreign selloff this year — $27.7 billion in outflows, surpassing 2025's record $18.9 billion — was partly driven by funds rotating into AI-linked stocks and away from markets with limited AI exposure, like India.

Foreign Flows and the HSBC Upgrade

There is a counterweight. HSBC upgraded Indian equities to "neutral" from "underweight" last week, raising its 2026 Sensex year-end target to 84,000 — suggesting an 8.6% upside from current levels. The move followed a similar upgrade from Goldman Sachs earlier this month.

Foreign investors have bought $1.6 billion in Indian shares so far in July, turning into net buyers after four months of heavy selling. But HSBC cautioned that the sustainability of these inflows is a key concern, especially if attention shifts back to AI-linked opportunities or the Middle East situation deteriorates further.

What to Watch

Key triggers for the week: Reliance Industries and ICICI Bank earnings, China's Loan Prime Rate decision on Monday, India's foreign exchange reserves data on Friday, and the US flash PMI readings that will signal whether American manufacturing is holding up. Technically, analysts peg Nifty resistance at 24,300–24,500, with support near 23,800–24,000.

The bigger picture remains unchanged: India's economic growth story is intact, but the market needs either the Iran conflict to de-escalate or a monsoon recovery to break out of its range. Until then, expect choppy, headline-driven sessions.
